title: Anyone can build it with AI; the difference is depth
introduction: No class on Tuesday: Boyd called us into his office one by one for a personal-tutor check-in, and the rest of the day was for preparing Thursday's crit. Wednesday was Ross's first Python workshop. Thursday is the Project 1 crit, with a guest artist, Orna, who works with holograms and immersive projection. This post is about the twenty-minute conversation and what I decided because of it, plus what I learned on Wednesday.
related_work: Boyd set out the rest of the term. The crit is not about a perfect project: 'it's about getting you a project that you can continue to develop, identifying the gaps in knowledge.' After this week the module moves into projection mapping with TouchDesigner, Unity and Blender, towards real-time visuals that respond to sound and to the room. The Python workshops run alongside.
method:
In the one-to-one I told him the truth: Project 0 and Project 1 both changed plan close to the deadline, both ended with two or three days of drawing, and both broke my sleep. I came in with no coding background and have used AI as a teacher. Boyd said I am progressing well and that this is his way of teaching: make a big project first, with AI if necessary, and go back for the technique afterwards. Then two rules for Project 2 and 3. 'Work in a more prototype fashion': grab any image from the web as a placeholder, and make original material only once the concept is fixed. And 'allow your initial work to be ugly': fast and rough until the idea works, beautiful last. The sentence that stayed with me: with AI, anyone can now make a website or a game. What cannot be generated is an interesting, critical concept. That is where the value is.

Wednesday was the Python workshop. Ross gave us a four-page handout with eighteen steps and we typed through all of them: a virtual environment in VS Code, hello.py, variables and the four types, input() with int() and str(), operators, if/elif/else as an age discount, for and while loops, lists and nested lists, functions, a recursive Fibonacci and the random module. He closed by opening TouchDesigner and showing a sphere whose points jump every frame because a Python script 'loops through them and adds a random offset'. TouchDesigner scripts are Python, and Project 2 will live there. Nothing was new in concept after p5; what was new was how Python punishes small things. I lost time to four mistakes, all whitespace or naming: one leading space on every line of operators.py gave four errors before anything ran; a print(total) indented too deep ran inside the loop; a file named random.py imported itself; and I pressed Insert and typed over my own code. None of this is Python knowledge; it is the habit of reading the editor before the error.
results_discussion: So I asked the uncomfortable question about Project 1: what is it, honestly? Two strangers, a hand gesture each, and a childhood assembled out of silhouettes and a picture book whose colours run away like sand. It is warm, and warmth is the problem; nothing in it makes anyone want to argue. The argument was already inside the work, I just had not said it. The childhood on screen is written in the present: two people who never met use today's mood to compose a past neither of them lived, and it still looks true. Memory is reconstructed, not retrieved (Bartlett, 1932; Boym's reflective nostalgia). And the silhouettes let everyone recognise themselves only because every detail has been removed, the shadow taken for the thing, as in Plato's cave that Sean Cubitt returned to on Tuesday. The sentence I will stand behind on Thursday: childhood is not found; it is co-written in the present, by two people, out of shadows.
conclusion_future_work: For Project 2 I have a direction, not a method: a flock or particle system in TouchDesigner, projected, responding to sound. The order will change: concept and critical question first, sent to Boyd before anything is produced; then the whole pipeline with placeholder images; original material last, in one go. The aim is a project I can explain for ten minutes without mentioning how it was built. The crit itself, what the room saw and what Boyd said, is written up as a Project 1 entry under Projects.
